paragraphs.text: The rest of the acts of Pekahiah during the period of his rule are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.

entries.section: (6) Pekah as king over Israel

paragraphs.text: Pekah’s installing himself as king over Israel was in the fifty-second year of Azariah king of Judah. He reigned in Samaria and his rule continued twenty years, but Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria reigned eighteen years and was a contemporary of Pekahiah and Pekah and, after him, Hoshea, kings of Israel. So the period of twenty years is not the period of his rule on the throne of Israel, but was during the former kings Pekahiah and Menahem and before them, since he was a commander in the army and the real force moving the kingdom.

entries.section: (6) Pekah as king over Israel

paragraphs.text: He did all the evils that his fathers had done before and did not refrain from walking in the ways of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who drew Israel after him to spiritual and moral destruction.

entries.section: (6) Pekah as king over Israel

paragraphs.text: Ijon: a fortified city of the children of Naphtali in the northern part of Palestine. It is now the village of Dibbin in southern Lebanon, near Marj Ayoun.

Abel-beth-maachah: a fortified city in Naphtali. Its place today is “Tell Abel,” a village west of the Jordan. Janoah: a city in Naphtali, the present “Yanuh,” ten kilometers east of Tyre. Kedesh: a fortified city of Naphtali in Galilee, now the village of “Qadas,” sixteen kilometers north of Safed.
Hazor: it was the capital of the Canaanites in northern Palestine. It lay above the waters of Merom.
It was given to the tribe of Naphtali. At present it is “Tell al-Qadah,” about six kilometers west of the Bridge of the Daughters of Jacob.
Gilead: a mountainous region east of the Jordan.
Galilee: a province in the mountainous region of Naphtali.
The land of Naphtali: in the northern part of the land of Palestine, bounded on the east by the Sea of Tiberias and the Jordan, and on the west by the land of Issachar and Zebulun.

The First Book of Chronicles tells us (1 Chr 5:26) that the kings of Assyria Pul and Tiglath-pileser attacked the tribes of the children of Israel, the Reubenites and the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh, and took their cities and carried them away captive and transported them and scattered them throughout the Assyrian kingdom. And it tells us here in this verse of another attack of Tiglath-pileser on the tribe of Naphtali, and he took from it the lands mentioned here and seized them and scattered their inhabitants in the cities of Assyria, so they became slaves in captivity.

We understand from this that Assyria’s taking of the kingdom of Israel came in three stages. We mentioned two stages here; as for the third stage, they occupied the rest of the cities of Israel, and the northern kingdom ended after King Hoshea, who followed King Pekah.

Satan your enemy keeps attacking you until you fall into his hand, so do not submit to him if he fights you, but take refuge in God quickly and resist him, and he will flee from you, and be sure that the power of God which is with you is stronger than Satan, so do not be troubled by your weakness.

entries.section: (6) Pekah as king over Israel

paragraphs.text: Conspiracy came to prevail again, and Hoshea the son of Elah rebelled against Pekah the son of Remaliah and assassinated him and seized the throne of Israel in the twentieth year of Jotham the son of Uzziah.
What is meant by the twentieth year is from the beginning of the reign of Jotham, and it is to be noted that Jotham reigned only sixteen years, that is, four years after the death of Jotham.

entries.section: (6) Pekah as king over Israel

paragraphs.text: The rest of the acts of Pekah are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.

entries.section: (7) Jotham as king over Judah

paragraphs.text: Jotham ascended the throne of Judah, succeeding his father Uzziah. That was in the second year of Pekah the son of Remaliah king of Israel, because Pekah reigned in the last year of the reign of Uzziah (v. 27) and in the following year, that is, the second year, when Uzziah died, his son Jotham reigned. It should be noted that this is the sole reign of Jotham, but it was preceded by several years in which he reigned with Uzziah his father, because of his leprosy and his isolation from dwelling in Jerusalem.

entries.section: (7) Jotham as king over Judah

paragraphs.text: Jotham was twenty-five years of age when he became king, and his rule in Jerusalem lasted sixteen years. His mother was Jerusha the daughter of Zadok.
We notice here, as we mentioned before, how great is the influence of a godly mother on her children. For the very next verse tells us the conduct that Jotham followed, for he did all that was right.

entries.section: (7) Jotham as king over Judah

paragraphs.text: Jotham cared to keep the commandments of God and His worship and walked uprightly before Him, as his father Uzziah had walked, and learned from him to live with God, but he guarded against the errors of his father, which were pride and entering the altar of incense in the Holy Place among the priests.

entries.section: (7) Jotham as king over Judah

paragraphs.text: Among the good works of Jotham was not only his holding fast to the commandments and the worship, but he also cared for the Temple of God, and so he built the higher gate, which was most likely a gate facing the north side of the Temple, through which came the animals that were to be slaughtered for God. But among the errors of Jotham is that, like most of the kings of Judah, he let the people sacrifice on the high places and did not limit sacrifice to the bronze altar of the Temple of God.

entries.section: (7) Jotham as king over Judah

paragraphs.text: The rest of what Jotham did is written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah, which is not the Book of Chronicles found in the Holy Bible. But the Second Book of Chronicles (2 Chr 27) tells us that Jotham cared to build many buildings beside the Temple and also cared for the fortifications of Jerusalem, because of the danger of an attack by Aram or Assyria.
Know that every good work you do is very precious to God, so be careful to do good and help the needy and care for the house of the Lord.

entries.section: (7) Jotham as king over Judah

paragraphs.text: At the end of the days of the rule of Jotham, Aram began to ally itself with Israel to make war on the kingdom of Judah, and although King Jotham was good, the people were corrupt and did not submit to the king (2 Chr 27:2); therefore the Lord wanted to chastise them, and so He allowed Aram and Israel to begin military skirmishes and they moved toward the kingdom of Judah, but no complete actual war took place until after the death of Jotham and the reign of his son Ahaz; for God, for the sake of the goodness of Jotham, postponed these attacks to the age of his son, the wicked King Ahaz.
And in this we notice the goodness of Jotham for the following reasons:
1- The godliness of his mother Jerusha, who cared to bring him up well.
2- His concern to do what is upright, by keeping the commandments and the holy acts of worship.
3- He cared for the Temple of God, and so he built the higher gate of the Temple and set up many buildings on the high place beside the Temple.
4- He cared to fortify Jerusalem, that the kingdom of Judah might be strong before the attacks of enemies.
5- He guarded against the errors of his father, and so he was humble and did not try to break the Law and enter the Holy Place. As for the errors of Jotham, they appear in the following:
1- His permitting and continuing the offering of sacrifices to God on the high places.

2- He was occupied with building works instead of bringing up his sons, and so Ahaz his son turned out wicked, and when he reigned evil prevailed in the kingdom, and perhaps Jotham married a wicked wife, the mother of Ahaz, who helped in the going astray of her son.

entries.section: (7) Jotham as king over Judah

paragraphs.text: Jotham died and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and his son Ahaz reigned in his place. Ahaz king of Judah

entries.section: (1) The reign of Ahaz over Judah

paragraphs.text: In the seventeenth year of Pekah the son of Remaliah king of Israel, Jehoahaz became king over Judah, after the death of Jotham his father. Because of his evil, the writer of the book removed the name of Jehovah, that is, God, from his name and called him Ahaz, because he worshiped idols. He began to reign at the age of twenty and reigned sixteen years, and we are told (ch. 18:2) that his son Hezekiah began to reign at the age of twenty-five. Of course Ahaz could not have begotten his son Hezekiah at the age of ten, because Ahaz died at the age of thirty-six, so that Ahaz would have been eleven years old when Hezekiah was born, that is, he would have begotten him at the age of ten. The truth is that Hezekiah reigned alone at the age of twenty-five, but he had reigned a period before that with his father, and his age then, when he began to reign, was less than twenty-five, perhaps twenty or fifteen; we do not know exactly, because the Holy Bible did not mention this. It was a custom among the kings to make their young sons kings with them, to secure the kingdom and to train them in managing the kingdom. And he did not do what was right like David his forefather the king, but walked in evil and the worship of idols.

entries.section: (1) The reign of Ahaz over Judah

paragraphs.text: Sadly, Ahaz imitated the kings of Israel, all of whom worshiped idols, and did not imitate his righteous father and forefather. So he served the god of the children of Ammon and offered his sons as burnt offerings to them, and not merely one son, as is mentioned here; for the Book of Chronicles mentions that he offered more than one son (2 Chr 28:3). And he worshiped the gods of the original inhabitants of the land, the pagans whom God drove out by the hand of Joshua, and offered sacrifices to the pagan gods on the high places and the hills and under the green trees which they had set apart for the worship of the pagan gods; that is, he went to extremes in the worship of the many pagan gods. His mention of every green tree shows how widespread the worship of idols was in the age of Ahaz; for he led his people astray and led them in the worship of idols.

And perhaps the reason for Ahaz’s going to extremes in the worship of idols was his fear of the alliance of Rezin king of Aram and Pekah the son of Remaliah king of Israel and their readiness to fight him; so instead of taking refuge in God, he took refuge in the pagan gods in great number, although Isaiah the prophet had reassured him that if he believed in God no harm would come to him (Isa 7:4-16), and that these two kings would die and their lands be forsaken, but he did not believe and lived in fear and the worship of idols. Likewise the prophet Micah rebuked him (Mic 6:6-8), because he offered his sons as burnt offerings to the god Molech, but he did not repent.

Do not reject the warnings and admonitions of God to you, whether in the Holy Bible, or from your father of confession and all those around you, lest you be exposed to error and destruction and live in fear and turmoil. Believe in the power of God which is with you, and you will live in tranquility.

entries.section: (2) Aram and Israel attack Judah

paragraphs.text: Rezin king of Aram and Pekah the son of Remaliah king of Israel feared Assyria, and so they united together to be a power that Assyria could not overcome, and they tried to unite with Ahaz king of Judah, but he refused, because of his inclination to rely on Assyria. So Rezin and Pekah rose against him to fight him and were able to be victorious over him in part, killing some of his soldiers (2 Chr 28:5-8), and they besieged Jerusalem, but they were not able to overcome him completely, and so they withdrew.

entries.section: (2) Aram and Israel attack Judah

paragraphs.text: During the invasions of Rezin king of Aram into the kingdom of Judah, he was able to take Elath, which is an important port on the Gulf of Aqaba at its northern end, the present Eilat, and he drove the Jews out of it and settled the Arameans in it.

entries.section: (2) Aram and Israel attack Judah

paragraphs.text: Ahaz was angered and afraid of the invasions of Aram and Israel, and instead of relying on God, he sent to the king of Assyria to ask his help, to protect him from the two kings of Aram and Israel.

This agreed with the ambitions of Assyria to take all the surrounding countries, and Ahaz’s request encouraged him to take the kingdom of Israel and Aram, and in this the captivity of the kingdom of Israel was accomplished; for the evils of Ahaz were a cause of the captivity of the northern kingdom. The weakness of Ahaz appears in his saying to the king of Assyria, “I am thy servant and thy son,” for he declares his complete submission to him. History does not mention that Ahaz was among the list of those who paid tribute to the king of Assyria, and this means that he was completely enslaved to him.

entries.section: (2) Aram and Israel attack Judah

paragraphs.text: As a declaration of his submission to the king of Assyria, Ahaz took the silver and gold that were in the house of the Lord and sent them as a present to the king of Assyria, that he might be pleased with him and protect him. This clearly confirms Ahaz’s reliance on the powers of the world and his lack of faith in God, so that he plundered the house of the Lord to please the pagan king of Assyria, and in this he halted the service in the house of the Lord; so he encourages and spreads the worship of idols and closes the house of the Lord and stops its worship.

entries.section: (2) Aram and Israel attack Judah

paragraphs.text: Kir: a city lying between the two rivers, and it is the original homeland of the Arameans.

The king of Assyria seized the opportunity to fulfill his ambitions, and so he answered the call of Ahaz, not out of love for him, but to fulfill his aims of taking the world around him, and he killed Rezin and took Damascus, the capital of the Arameans.

God wants to support you, so why do you look for other means and so expose yourself to troubles? Know that the world works for its own interest and not for your interest, and that God alone is the One who loves you and wants your salvation, so do not draw away from Him, however dangers surround you.

entries.section: (3) Ahaz and his new altar

paragraphs.text: Ahaz went to Damascus to congratulate the king of Assyria on his victories over the Arameans and to declare his submission to him, and he saw how the king of Assyria had taken control of the city and set up in it a great altar to the gods of the Assyrians, in order to break the identity, nationality and religion of the Arameans, so that they would worship the gods of the Assyrians. And because Ahaz did not care about the worship of God and worshiped idols, he flattered the king of Assyria by taking the form and dimensions of the Assyrian altar and sending them to Urijah the high priest, to make an altar like it inside the house of the Lord, although it was God who had given David in writing the details of building the Temple, and David handed them to Solomon, who carried them out exactly in obedience to the word of God (1 Chr 28:19); but Ahaz here despises God and His Temple to please the king of Assyria.

entries.section: (3) Ahaz and his new altar

paragraphs.text: Urijah the priest carried out all that Ahaz asked and built an altar according to the designs sent to him by King Ahaz. And he completed its building before the return of the king from Damascus. This shows the weakness of Urijah the high priest and his laxity in the right of God and His house to please the king. It also shows the weakness of the worship of God and of the priestly leadership in the days of Ahaz, and the going astray of the people after foreign gods. And we marvel before the faith of Naaman the Syrian, who took earth from the land of Israel to set up an altar to the Lord in Damascus, while Ahaz the Jew, who did not believe in God, sets up in the house of the Lord an altar after the pattern of the pagan altars.

entries.section: (3) Ahaz and his new altar

paragraphs.text: When Ahaz returned from Damascus he saw the great altar that he had charged Urijah the priest to build, and he admired it. And in pride that reaches beyond the priesthood, he came forward himself to offer a peace offering and himself sprinkled its blood on this altar, after he had offered his offering on this altar and poured out on it his drink offering of wine. Here he erred in two things:
1- His usurping the priesthood in offering the sacrifice.

2- Making an altar contrary to the commandments of God, which he set up after the pattern of the altars of the pagans, and he even set it up in place of the bronze altar of God and removed the other and put it aside, as we shall see in (v. 14).

entries.section: (3) Ahaz and his new altar

paragraphs.text: Ahaz set up the new great altar before the house of the Lord, which is on the east side; before it stood the bronze altar, then the Sea in which the priests washed, then the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies. So that the new altar might be the main altar and the sacrifices of the children of Israel be offered on it, Ahaz commanded that the bronze altar be removed and moved aside to the north side, that is, on the right of one entering the house of the Lord. This is a clear ritual violation, meaning Ahaz’s concern to please the king of Assyria instead of pleasing the Lord.

entries.section: (3) Ahaz and his new altar

paragraphs.text: King Ahaz commanded Urijah the priest to offer the morning burnt offering and the evening offering, and the king’s burnt offering and his offering, with the burnt offering of the people and their offering and the drink offerings of their wine, on the altar which he called the great altar. And it was set apart for sprinkling the blood of every burnt offering or sacrifice. As for the bronze altar, it would be for the king, when he wished to inquire of the Lord in some matter. This means Ahaz’s attempt to get rid of the bronze altar, by putting it aside and saying, if I want to ask God about something I will use this altar; in truth he wants to get rid of this altar, but after a while, so as not to stir up the priests and the people. And Urijah the priest did all that King Ahaz asked.

entries.section: (3) Ahaz and his new altar

paragraphs.text: After Ahaz had taken the gold and silver that were in the house of the Lord and worship in it was neglected and he had replaced the bronze altar with his great altar, he felt that the bronze Sea, in which the priests washed before entering the Holy Place, was unimportant, and likewise the ten lavers that Solomon had made for washing the sacrifices in them; for he in general was not concerned with worship in the house of the Lord but with all the worship of idols in the city of Jerusalem. Therefore he took the bronze bases on which the lavers rested and put the lavers on the ground. He also took the twelve bronze oxen on which the Sea rested; perhaps he wanted to make use of their bronze. And he put the Sea on a row of stones. In sum, Ahaz despised the house of the Lord and thought of his own interest and of acquiring bronze to benefit him in the costs of his kingdom.

entries.section: (3) Ahaz and his new altar

paragraphs.text: There was in the house of the Lord a large hall in which the people gathered on the Sabbath day for worship, and since Ahaz neglected the sanctification of the Sabbath day and the worship of God in His Temple, he removed this hall, that is, the covert. There was also a special entrance for the king from his house to the Temple of God, and he removed it too, because he did not want the worship of God in His Temple; all this was to please the king of Assyria, and in this Ahaz declares to him that he has neglected the worship of God and worships the gods of the Assyrians, for whom he had set up altars in all parts of Jerusalem.

If a person gives himself up to sin, he slips into its depths and does evils without limit, as Ahaz did. But you, O man of God, hold fast to the worship of God in His Church and beware of sin. And if you fall, repent quickly and return to God, and He will cleanse you from every evil, for He loves the weak and supports them but is greatly angered at the rebellious and those who take liberties.

entries.section: (4) The death of Ahaz and the reign of Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: The rest of what Ahaz did during the period of his rule is written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah. Ahaz died and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and his son Hezekiah reigned after him. The evils of Ahaz were very many and were written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah, which, as we mentioned, is not the Book of Chronicles found in the Holy Bible. We notice that because of the multitude of the evils of Ahaz he was not buried in the tombs of the kings of Judah, but was buried in ordinary graves in the city of David (2 Chr 28:27). And God allowed this king to die young, for he died at the age of thirty-six, so that Judah might be rid of his many evils.

In the age of the wicked Ahaz lived the great prophet Isaiah, to proclaim the voice of God. So be assured that God does not leave Himself without a witness, and do not be troubled by the multitude of evils around you. Be faithful in obeying the commandments of God and know that there are many who still worship God as you do, so complete your striving that you may receive the Kingdom. The captivity of Israel and the sins of the people of God

entries.section: (1) Hoshea and the captivity of Israel

paragraphs.text: Hoshea the son of Elah reigned over Israel in Samaria, after he assassinated Pekah the son of Remaliah, and the period of his rule lasted nine years, and that was in the twelfth year of King Ahaz, king of the children of Judah.

entries.section: (1) Hoshea and the captivity of Israel

paragraphs.text: He committed evils, but his conduct was less perverse than that of the kings of Israel who preceded him.

entries.section: (1) Hoshea and the captivity of Israel

paragraphs.text: Shalmaneser king of Assyria threatened him with invasion, and so Hoshea submitted to him and paid him tribute, that he might confirm him over the kingdom of Israel, and in this he became his vassal. That is because Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria was the one who made Hoshea king over Israel, as the history of Assyria mentions. Hoshea remained submissive to Assyria until the death of Tiglath-pileser, and after that he rebelled against Assyria, and Shalmaneser, the new king of Assyria, attacked him and subjected Hoshea to himself, and he paid tribute to Assyria.

entries.section: (1) Hoshea and the captivity of Israel

paragraphs.text: Hoshea remained far from God and relied on his own thinking in his rebellion against Assyria and then his submission to it, and so he thought of rebelling again against Shalmaneser and not paying him tribute, seizing the opportunity of Shalmaneser’s being occupied with fighting Phoenicia, that is, present-day Lebanon, and he sent to ally himself with the king of Egypt, who is called So. The king of Assyria discovered this alliance and the treachery of Hoshea, because he had not paid the tribute, so Shalmaneser sent and seized Hoshea and put him in prison, and the kingdom of Israel was left without a leader, which made it easier afterward, when Samaria was besieged, for it to fall into the hand of the Assyrians.

The prophet Hosea had warned King Hoshea against allying with So king of Egypt (Hos 7:11, 12:1), but he did not obey God, for he relied on human power, and the result was his humiliation in prison. The nine years of his reign are counted until the fall of Samaria and not until his being put in prison, that is, King Hoshea was put in prison in the sixth year of his reign.

entries.section: (1) Hoshea and the captivity of Israel

paragraphs.text: The king of Assyria attacked all the lands of Israel and went to Samaria, the capital, and besieged it for three years. And Shalmaneser died during the siege of Samaria and Sargon succeeded him, into whose hand Samaria fell. The kingdom of Israel was taken captive in three stages, which took sixty-five years, and they are:
1- The first attack at the hand of Tiglath-pileser, a year after the prophecy of Isaiah.
2- The second attack at the hand of Shalmaneser, twenty years after the prophecy of Isaiah.

3- The third and last attack at the hand of Esarhaddon, after a period of sixty-five years from the prophecy of Isaiah, and this was the complete captivity of Israel. During that time Manasseh king of Judah was seized and imprisoned in Babylon for a period, and then he pardoned him and returned him to Jerusalem. The Assyrian writings mention that Shalmaneser took captive 27,290 of Israel and took fifty war chariots.

entries.section: (1) Hoshea and the captivity of Israel

paragraphs.text: Halah: the name of a province in the empire of Assyria, in Mesopotamia, near the town of Gozan. Habor, the river of Gozan: a river in Mesopotamia, the river Khabur, which flows south through Mesopotamia and after 300 km meets the eastern branch of the Euphrates. Media: a land lying east of Assyria, now part of present-day Iran.

In the ninth year of Hoshea the king of Assyria took Samaria and carried the children of Israel captive and sent them to the countries subject to the kingdom of Assyria and settled them in several cities: Halah, and Habor by the river of Gozan, and the cities of the Medes.

The Holy Bible does not mention when Hoshea died, because he was a wicked king; God did not care to record his death and burial, and of course no king succeeded him over Israel, because it had come to an end as a kingdom and had become a province subject to the kingdom of Assyria.

When you feel your weakness before the powers of the world, take refuge in God and do not look for human solutions; they alone will not benefit you if God does not bless them, for He is the source of your protection and your strength and the salvation of your soul.

entries.section: (2) The sins of the children of Israel before the captivity

paragraphs.text: It may seem at first sight that the captivity of Israel took place because of the power of Assyria, which swept over the world around it and took many countries, among them the kingdom of Israel. But the true cause of the captivity of Israel is its sins. These verses mention a list of the sins of Israel and also of the kingdom of Judah, which fell some time after it, also because of its sins. And the first sin it mentions is that after God had freed them from the slavery of Egypt and its idols, they returned and worshiped the foreign gods, in addition to their worship of God.

entries.section: (2) The sins of the children of Israel before the captivity

paragraphs.text: And since the children of Israel mixed with the nations and worshiped their gods and also took from them their pagan customs and their evil forms of worship, they added to these evils their following and encouraging of their wicked kings, beginning with Jeroboam, who split the kingdom of Israel, that is, the ten tribes, and set up the idols in Bethel and Dan, and then all the kings of Israel followed him, down to Hoshea, the last of their kings, for all of them worshiped idols and some of them went to extremes in these pagan forms of worship, such as Ahab.

entries.section: (2) The sins of the children of Israel before the captivity

paragraphs.text: The tower of the watchmen: a small farm with a watchtower.

The worship of idols began among the children of Israel secretly in their houses, or in hiding, and then it spread, and the children of Israel went to extremes in their evil, and offered worship to the foreign gods on the high places. And these strange forms of worship spread throughout all the land of the children of Israel, from the very smallest village to the large fortified city.

Be on your guard against sin when it creeps in on you, for it enters your thought first, and then it comes by way of sight or thought, and presses on you and changes your speech, and then defiles your deeds and enslaves you. So drive sin out from its beginning by repentance and by keeping away from the sources of evil, however dear they are in your sight.

entries.section: (2) The sins of the children of Israel before the captivity

paragraphs.text: They made idols and poles on the hills and under every large tree with wide shade; that is, pagan worship continued to spread until it was in every place.

entries.section: (2) The sins of the children of Israel before the captivity

paragraphs.text: The people of God offered complete acts of worship to the idols by offering sacrifices and burning incense, and indeed they did, like the nations whom God drove out before them, vile evils to please the idols, such as fornication and every uncleanness. In this they defied God by their disobedience and provoked Him; for God had commanded them clearly in the Law of Moses to keep away from the worship of idols (Ex 20:1-5).

entries.section: (2) The sins of the children of Israel before the captivity

paragraphs.text: The seer: one who sees visions, by which God makes known to him His commands, to deliver them to the people.
The Lord sent to Israel and Judah many prophets and seers, calling them to leave their evil practices and to walk according to the commandments of the Lord, His statutes and the judgments of His Law.

entries.section: (2) The sins of the children of Israel before the captivity

paragraphs.text: They hardened their necks: that is, they turned their backs to God and were stubborn against Him. The expression is taken from an animal, such as a horse, that stiffens its neck so that the rider cannot lead it.
They did not heed the calls and warnings of the prophets, but continued in their error and went to extremes in their stubbornness, like their fathers, who refused to believe in the Lord their God.

entries.section: (2) The sins of the children of Israel before the captivity

paragraphs.text: His statutes: His acts of worship.
His covenant: that He would be their God and they would be His people.
His testimonies: His commandments and His Law.

The children of Israel refused to submit to their covenant with God, to be a special people who worship Him alone. And they left His worship and His commandments, which they transgressed, and these bore witness to their perversion. And they followed the nations in the worship of the foreign, vain gods, which profit nothing, and so they became a perverted people, of no value, like the rest of the nations, and they lost the blessing of God and His protection of them. And because the worship of idols is vain, whoever worships idols becomes vain himself, that is, without value.

entries.section: (2) The sins of the children of Israel before the captivity

paragraphs.text: The two calves: that is, the two idols that Jeroboam the son of Nebat set up in the kingdom of Israel, in Bethel and Dan.
Groves: the plural of grove, which is a tall pole set up on the high places for the worship of the moon, with altars built beside this pole.
The host of heaven: the heavenly bodies and stars which the Assyrians worship.
Baal: one of the most famous pagan gods in the land of Canaan, and the sun was a symbol of him.

Israel neglected the commandments of God and His worship in His Temple in Jerusalem and worshiped the golden calves in Bethel and Dan, in addition to the gods of the nations, and so they set up poles and temples for them.

entries.section: (2) The sins of the children of Israel before the captivity

paragraphs.text: The people of God plunged into the worship of idols, and so they burned their sons in the fire to please Molech the god of the children of Ammon, and they sought the unseen through diviners and sorcerers, who deal with demons, and they felt that good or evil would come upon them from strange things, such as the falling of a morsel from the mouth or the passing of a gazelle across the road; that is, they took omens of good and of evil, and in this they sold themselves to evil, that is, became slaves of the pagan gods, and provoked God.
All these demonic practices still influence some societies around us, so let us avoid them completely, for the Scripture warns us against them in the strongest warning (Deut 18:10-12).

entries.section: (2) The sins of the children of Israel before the captivity

paragraphs.text: Because of all these evils God was angry with His people in the kingdom of Israel and allowed Assyria to take them captive, and only the kingdom of Judah remained, because it still worshiped God in His Temple in Jerusalem, even if it sometimes fell into the worship of idols, and so God gave it another opportunity to repent. But it did not repent, and He allowed its captivity a hundred and thirty-five years later at the hand of Babylon. And the word of God about the kingdom of Israel, that He removed them out of His sight, is the hardest thing, that is, the protection and blessing of God left them and He refused to dwell among them, and so He scattered them among the nations to humble them, that perhaps they might repent.

entries.section: (2) The sins of the children of Israel before the captivity

paragraphs.text: After God gave the kingdom of Judah an opportunity to repent, sadly it did as the kingdom of Israel did and worshiped idols, and did not learn from the captivity of Israel and did not fear God, and so it halted between the worship of God and the worship of idols.

entries.section: (2) The sins of the children of Israel before the captivity

paragraphs.text: The Lord rejected all the children of Israel and punished them, delivering them into the hand of spoilers and casting them out of His sight.

entries.section: (2) The sins of the children of Israel before the captivity

paragraphs.text: Jeroboam the son of Nebat split off with the ten tribes and set up a kingdom which he called Israel, and the kingdom of Judah remained under the rule of the descendants of David. With the separation of the kingdom of Israel it walked in the worship of idols and began to draw away from God, until its captivity to Assyria was accomplished.

entries.section: (2) The sins of the children of Israel before the captivity

paragraphs.text: By the children of Israel is meant the people of God in the kingdom of Israel, who worshiped the golden calves that Jeroboam set up; that is, the people continued in the worship of idols until God allowed their captivity, that is, He turned His face away from them and abandoned them, as He had warned them many times by the mouth of His prophets, before this Assyrian captivity was accomplished. But in the end, because of their insistence on provoking God, He was compelled to leave them to captivity and humiliation, that perhaps they might repent.

entries.section: (3) The worship of God and of idols after the captivity

paragraphs.text: Babylon: a city on both banks of the river Euphrates; its region was anciently known as the land of Shinar. Cuth: a city belonging to Babylon, lying twenty-four kilometers northeast of Babylon. Ava: a Babylonian city.
Hamath: a city on the Orontes river north of Hermon, about one hundred and ninety kilometers north of Damascus.
Sepharvaim: a town lying on both banks of the river Euphrates, twenty-six kilometers southwest of Baghdad.

The king of Assyria removed the children of Israel from the cities of Samaria and settled them in the cities that Assyria controlled, and brought people from Assyrian cities: Babylon, Cuth, Ava, Hamath and Sepharvaim. And he settled them in the cities of Samaria instead of the children of Israel, and they dwelt in its cities.

That was the policy of some empires in earlier times, which aimed at mixing the peoples with one another, in order to guard against the feeling of nationhood and attachment to the land; that is, the kings of Assyria, in their three invasions of the kingdom of Israel, did this, and so did their successors among the kings of Assyria.

entries.section: (3) The worship of God and of idols after the captivity

paragraphs.text: After a large number of the Jews were deported to the land of Assyria and a number of the inhabitants of the land of Assyria were settled in their place, the number of inhabitants became fewer and the land was wide for them, so the number of lions in the land increased, and this was by the permission of God, and they devoured some of them and they were very afraid. This was a divine chastening of the pagans, that they might understand that this land has a God whom they ought to obey, for they are pagans who believe in a plurality of gods. And we notice that they were able to understand that there is a mighty God of this land, and they feared Him. But on the other hand the Jews, who knew that God is the owner of all lands, did not fear Him and neglected His commandments and worshiped the foreign gods, and so God drove them out of His land.

If only you would learn from all those around you, for you may find in some who are far from God virtues that you need to learn, and even to go deeper in them, because you have an opportunity, by the power of God, to master them. And according to the measure of your humility and your love of being a disciple, God will give to you.

entries.section: (3) The worship of God and of idols after the captivity

paragraphs.text: They sent to the king of Assyria, saying that the people whom he had brought to the cities of Samaria to settle there did not know the ordinances of the god of this land, and so he sent lions among them which devoured them. There was a belief among the ancient pagan peoples that every land has its god, whom it must worship.

entries.section: (3) The worship of God and of idols after the captivity

paragraphs.text: The king of Assyria commanded that one of the priests whom they had carried away captive from that land be sent there, to return to Samaria and dwell there and teach the new settlers the ordinances of the god of the land. This priest was not one of the priests of God of the descendants of Aaron, but one of the priests of the calves that Jeroboam the son of Nebat set up; he was Jewish in origin and knew God and the books of Moses, but did not have the rank of the priesthood, so his information about God was confused, but he knew about God better than the nations, who did not know Him at all.

entries.section: (3) The worship of God and of idols after the captivity

paragraphs.text: One of the captive priests who had been taken from Samaria did indeed come and returned there and dwelt in Bethel and taught them how they should fear the Lord and what His ordinances were. And Bethel is where one of the calves that Jeroboam the son of Nebat set up was found. This priest may have been from Bethel, and so he taught them the Law of Moses but also taught them the worship of the golden calf.

entries.section: (3) The worship of God and of idols after the captivity

paragraphs.text: Each of those foreign nations made the idols of its gods and put them in the temples which the Samaritans had built on the hills, each nation in the cities in which it was settled. And so they worshiped God and held to the Law of Moses, but at the same time worshiped their idols; that is, they considered God a god among the gods, respected Him and feared Him and also cared for the rest of the gods, who are demons.

And we notice here that this is the first mention of the title Samaritans, that is, the inhabitants of Samaria and its surroundings, who were the dwellers in all of the kingdom of Israel, and the Jews who lived in Jerusalem and Judea shunned them and despised them, because in their worship they associated the pagan gods with God.
The Samaritans were of three kinds:
1- Samaritans of Jewish origin who were content with the worship of God and of the two calves that Jeroboam the son of Nebat set up; these were few in number.
2- Samaritans of Jewish origin who worshiped the two calves and added to them other pagan gods whom they worshiped.
3- Samaritans of Gentile origin who worshiped their foreign gods and added to them the worship of God; these were many in number.

We also see that the new inhabitants in the cities of Samaria found old houses built on the high places, which the Jews, the inhabitants of the kingdom of Israel, had built in violation of the Law of God, and so they offered to God on the high places and also to the pagan gods.

entries.section: (3) The worship of God and of idols after the captivity

paragraphs.text: Succoth-benoth: a pagan god, the name meaning the tabernacles of the daughters, that is, the tents of the girls consecrated to fornication in the pagan temples, and it is symbolized by a hen with her chicks.
Nergal: the god of war and plague among the Babylonians; his statue is in the form of a lion with two wings and the face of a man. Ashima: he is the god of fire.
Nibhaz: a pagan god whose statue is half dog and half man.
Adrammelech: the god of the sun, symbolized by the mule.
Anammelech: the god of the moon, symbolized by the horse.
The new inhabitants in the cities of Samaria worshiped their pagan gods mentioned here and added to them the worship of God.

entries.section: (3) The worship of God and of idols after the captivity

paragraphs.text: Thus they worshiped the Lord, but at the same time they set up from among themselves priests to serve in the temples of the hills, and they offered their burnt offerings in them. Their worship of God was outward, out of fear of the lions, and was mixed with pagan forms of worship; it was not real godliness toward God but superficial worship, for they did not know God. And this is what Christ said in His conversation with the Samaritan woman, that they worship what they do not know (Jn 4:22).

entries.section: (3) The worship of God and of idols after the captivity

paragraphs.text: The nations that came to the cities of Samaria outwardly worshiped God, but in truth they did not fear Him nor follow the statutes and ordinances, that is, the acts of worship and the commandments which the Jews perform, in addition to their mixing the superficial worship of God with the worship of idols, whereas God commanded in His commandments that He alone be worshiped.

entries.section: (3) The worship of God and of idols after the captivity

paragraphs.text: The Lord had made a covenant in former days with the children of Israel and commanded them not to worship other gods, not to bow down to them nor fear them nor offer sacrifices to them, but to fear the Lord alone, who brought them out of Egypt with great power and might; to Him alone they bow down and to Him alone they offer their burnt offerings. This is what the nations ought to have done when they wished to worship God, to become Jews and hold to all His commandments, but they did not do so, and their worship was superficial worship.

entries.section: (3) The worship of God and of idols after the captivity

paragraphs.text: So those who believe in God must obey the statutes, the ordinances, the Law and the commandments that He gave them, to apply them all the days of their life and not to worship other gods.

entries.section: (3) The worship of God and of idols after the captivity

paragraphs.text: And they must always remember the covenant He made with them and not worship other gods, but must fear the Lord their God alone, and He will save them and protect them from all their enemies.

entries.section: (3) The worship of God and of idols after the captivity

paragraphs.text: But those foreign nations refused to listen and continued to practice their old rites, worshiping the Lord outwardly on the one hand and worshiping their idols on the other, and their sons followed this evil conduct, until the time of the writing of this book.

The fear of the Lord cannot be united with the paganism of the world. The fear of the Lord means obeying Him, and obedience to the Lord does not tolerate a mixing of complete submission to His will with the love of the world.
Hezekiah king over Judah

entries.section: (1) The reign of Hezekiah and his reforms

paragraphs.text: Hezekiah became king over Judah at the age of twenty-five, and that was in the third year of Hoshea the son of Elah king of Israel, and he reigned in Jerusalem, and his reign lasted twenty-nine years. His mother’s name was Abi, the daughter of Zechariah.

Hezekiah began to reign in the third year of Hoshea, that is, the fifteenth year of the reign of his father Ahaz; for it is mentioned that Hoshea began to reign in the twelfth year of Ahaz (ch. 17:1), although it is mentioned in (ch. 16:2) that Ahaz reigned sixteen years. The difference of a year between fifteen and sixteen is because parts of a year are sometimes counted and sometimes not counted. This is the time of Hezekiah’s reigning alone, after the death of his father Ahaz, but he had reigned a period with him before his death, as was the custom of some kings in this time, to prepare their sons for the kingship. And it is beautiful that Hezekiah, despite his living with his wicked father Ahaz, did not imitate him in his evil but quietly held fast to the commandments of God until he reigned alone and had the authority, and then his goodness and his spiritual reforms appeared, and he was obedient to the commands of God which he heard from Isaiah the prophet, whereas his father neglected the words of Isaiah.

entries.section: (1) The reign of Hezekiah and his reforms

paragraphs.text: His works were good, and he followed in the footsteps of his great forefather David in his righteousness. It is not said of the kings of Judah that they were good and perfect like David, except of three, the first of whom is Asa (1 Kgs 15:11), then Hezekiah, and in the end Josiah (2 Kgs 22:1, 2). The brilliance of these three appears in that they were righteous, although their fathers were wicked.

And we find that it was said of these three that they did what was right like David their father; this is true repentance, that is, returning to the right position in the relationship with God. David represents the pure relationship to which a person should return when he repents, so that he becomes completely upright in the eyes of the Lord, and not merely partially upright, as we mentioned of some of the kings before Hezekiah in the series of the kings of Judah, such as Jotham, Uzziah and Amaziah.

entries.section: (1) The reign of Hezekiah and his reforms

paragraphs.text: Nehushtan: a Hebrew word meaning a piece of bronze.

The Second Book of Chronicles tells us (2 Chr 29) that Hezekiah opened the house of the Lord and began to organize the worship in it and called the people to keep the Passover, and they returned to God. And Hezekiah removed the places of pagan worship on the hills and broke the images and cut down the poles and crushed the bronze serpent that Moses had made, because the children of Israel had burned incense to it, and they had called it Nehushtan.

God had commanded Moses to make this bronze serpent so that everyone bitten by the serpents might look at it and be healed (Num 21:8), and the children of Israel kept it because it signified a blessing. But when they sank low and worshiped idols, they considered this serpent an idol and worshiped it.

This shows the courage of Hezekiah and his holding fast to God, in that he did not fear the rebellion of the people, many of whom had become attached to the worship of idols in the days of his father, and he did not fear the king of Assyria either, who had commanded the spread of the worship of the idols of Assyria in Judah and in all the kingdom of Assyria; for it is said of Hezekiah that he “removed,” and he did not wait for the repentance of the people and their support of him, but removed the evil himself, and then the people returned to God and followed Hezekiah. He is thus a man of initiative and strong in his holding fast to God and his removal of evil.

We also notice how Satan was able to turn the bronze serpent, which signified the work and blessing of God, into an idol that the people worshiped when they drew away from God; for Satan is always crafty and deceitful and exploits a person’s distance from God to humiliate him.

entries.section: (1) The reign of Hezekiah and his reforms

paragraphs.text: Hezekiah relied on the power of God, and among the former kings of Israel there was none like him in his trust in God.
Your trust in God gives you tranquility and opens to you the doors of relationship and the sense of God and, consequently, righteous conduct, and so you also become an example to those around you.

entries.section: (1) The reign of Hezekiah and his reforms

paragraphs.text: He clave to the Lord and did not turn aside from His ways, but lived as the commandments required, which the Lord commanded Moses.

And we notice in (vv. 5, 6) that it was said of Hezekiah that he trusted in God and clave to Him and kept His commandments; for whoever believes in God and trusts in Him loves Him and clings to Him in prayers and readings of His word in the Holy Bible, and so he can easily keep His commandments and always strive to carry them out. Therefore believe in God, and you will love Him, and then you will keep His commandments.

entries.section: (1) The reign of Hezekiah and his reforms

paragraphs.text: Because of Hezekiah’s trust in the Lord and his removal of the worship of idols and his concern for the worship of God, God supported him in all his works, and he prospered in them, and in this Hezekiah rebelled against the king of Assyria and the worship of his idols. But Assyria did not attack him, because it was occupied with wars in other countries. God rejoiced in the uprightness of Hezekiah, but the people agreed with him, though not with all their heart, as shown by the fact that Isaiah, who was his contemporary, did not cease to rebuke them, because he knew the evil of their hearts, as appears from the whole prophecy of Isaiah.

entries.section: (1) The reign of Hezekiah and his reforms

paragraphs.text: From the tower of the watchmen to the fenced city: from the small farm to the large fortified city.

It seems that the king of Assyria had given some cities of Judah to the king of Gaza, and so Hezekiah fought the Philistines in their city Gaza and smote them and recovered the cities that had been seized from Judah. And God was with him, and he defeated the Philistines in their fortified cities and in their small unwalled villages.

We notice that Hezekiah’s rebellion against Assyria did not anger God, as shown by God’s support of Hezekiah against the Philistines, and then against Assyria, when He killed its armies by means of the king, as we shall see. But God was angry with Zedekiah, the last of the kings of Judah, because he did not obey Jeremiah the prophet, who told him to submit to Babylon, because it was a divine chastening and God had commanded this chastening (ch. 25:5-7).

entries.section: (2) The captivity of Israel

paragraphs.text: In the fourth year of King Hezekiah king of Judah, which corresponds to the seventh year of King Hoshea the son of Elah king of Israel, Shalmaneser king of Assyria threatened Samaria and his armies besieged it.

entries.section: (2) The captivity of Israel

paragraphs.text: The siege lasted three years, after which the city surrendered and the king of Assyria occupied it. That was in the sixth year of Hezekiah, which corresponds to the ninth year of Hoshea.

entries.section: (2) The captivity of Israel

paragraphs.text: The king of Assyria carried the children of Israel captive and led them to Assyria and settled them in the cities subject to his authority, which are Halah and Habor by the river of Gozan, and also in the cities of the Medes (see the previous chapter for the identification of those cities).

entries.section: (2) The captivity of Israel

paragraphs.text: This severe blow to the people of Israel was a chastening for them from the Lord, because they had stopped their ears to His warnings and broken His covenant, and all that Moses commanded them they did not heed and did not do, but worshiped idols and followed their evil lusts and provoked God.
It is clear that Hezekiah benefited from the captivity of Israel and their bondage, for he increased in his clinging to God and in his removal of pagan forms of worship.

Learn from the errors of others so that you guard against them, and so keep away from the sources of evil and fear God and worship Him, and you will live in tranquility and peace and God will prosper you in your works.

entries.section: (3) Assyria takes the cities of Judah and takes tribute

paragraphs.text: After the final destruction of Israel by Shalmaneser king of Assyria, his successor Sennacherib attacked all the fortified cities of Judah and took them. That was in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah.

entries.section: (3) Assyria takes the cities of Judah and takes tribute

paragraphs.text: Lachish: a fortified city in the kingdom of Judah, lying west of Hebron, fifteen miles away.
A talent of silver: it has several weights ranging between 20 and 40 kg.
A talent of gold: equal to 17.4 kg.

Despite the uprightness of Hezekiah’s heart, his faith was shaken when he found that Sennacherib king of Assyria had taken the fortified cities of Judah. Consequently there remained before him only the taking of Jerusalem, and he feared the Assyrian attack and did not rely on God, so he sent to Sennacherib to apologize to him for not submitting to him and to beg him to leave the cities of Judah, in return for paying him the tribute that he would fix. So Sennacherib fixed a heavy tribute on Hezekiah, three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold. But sadly Sennacherib betrayed the agreement and attacked Jerusalem afterward, and these are the characteristics of the wicked. This was so that Hezekiah might learn to rely on God alone and not make agreements with the wicked.

Be loving to all people, but do not arrange your life on the basis of your relationship with the wicked. Keep away from them and pray for them with love and deal with them in a limited way and rely on God, and He will protect you from them. Be ready to help them if they are in need, but do not trust them nor rely on them.

entries.section: (3) Assyria takes the cities of Judah and takes tribute

paragraphs.text: The tribute was very great, and so Hezekiah was compelled to take all the silver found in the treasury of the house of the Lord.

entries.section: (3) Assyria takes the cities of Judah and takes tribute

paragraphs.text: In order to pay the gold that he owed, Hezekiah did not find enough in his treasuries or the treasuries of the house of the Lord, and so he was compelled to strip the gold from the doors and the pillars of the house of the Lord and send it to Sennacherib.

entries.section: (4) Assyria’s threats against Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: The conduit of the upper pool, which is in the highway of the fuller’s field: a conduit lying outside the walls of Jerusalem and beside them and reaching inside the walls to a pool inside the city, to supply the city with water; this conduit is beside the fuller’s field, the fuller being one who whitens cloth. They say that there was a statue of this fuller until the seventh century, and this conduit lies north of the city of Jerusalem.

Sennacherib betrayed the agreement with Hezekiah, for after taking the very great tribute he also attacked Jerusalem with a great army and sent two of the commanders of his army, and the third, the king’s cupbearer and his spokesman, because he spoke Hebrew well, to King Hezekiah, demanding that he surrender the city and not rely on his God.

entries.section: (4) Assyria’s threats against Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: The recorder: the historian.

When the men of Sennacherib called to King Hezekiah from outside the walls, he sent out to them three of the officers who assisted him, and they stood on the wall to confer with the commanders of the army of Sennacherib.

entries.section: (4) Assyria’s threats against Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: Vain words: that is, you have no power but words with which to defend yourself in war.
Strength for the war: power with which to fight.

Rabshakeh, the official spokesman in the name of King Sennacherib, spoke, addressing the men of Hezekiah who stood on the wall, to deliver to him the message of Sennacherib, who rebuked Hezekiah, declaring to him his weakness, for he had nothing but mere words. How can he rely on words and rebel against the great king of Assyria, the conqueror of all the kingdoms of the earth?

From this the pride of Sennacherib and his men appears, and their contempt for God and His children and His city Jerusalem. For they regard the faith of Hezekiah and his people as mere words, resting on nothing, because they do not believe in the power of God.

Do not be troubled by the threats of the wicked, for they do not know the power of your God, who protects you; you are stronger with God than all their power and authority. Stand firm in your faith and principles, and you will see with your own eyes their shaking, for they are mere words without power, and Satan and his followers are nothing before the power of God, on whom you rely.

entries.section: (4) Assyria’s threats against Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: A bruised reed: a stick of cane that has been struck and is almost broken.
Sennacherib rebuked Hezekiah, thinking that he had relied on Egypt and for this reason rebelled against Assyria, although this had not happened, because Hezekiah relied on God and not on men.

And he likened Egypt, in mockery, to a bruised reed, that is, very weak, so that if someone leans on it, it does not support him, but because it is weak and has been struck, it will break and pierce his palm and wound it and pierce his hand. By this he means that relying on Egypt will harm everyone who relies on it, and this confirms the king of Assyria’s immersion in pride.

entries.section: (4) Assyria’s threats against Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: Continuing his casting of doubt on Hezekiah’s strength, Sennacherib said to him, if you have not relied on Egypt but have relied on God, know that God is angry with you, because you have broken down His altars. For Sennacherib, as a pagan king, does not know the difference between the temples of the idols, which Hezekiah removed, and the altar of God, which is in His Temple, and so he said to Hezekiah that you have removed the altars of God and left one altar, and of course this angers Him and He will not support you against me. Sennacherib feels that what Hezekiah says, in his reliance on God, is deceit, because as a pagan who believes in a plurality of gods, how can one tear down the altars of the gods and yet rely on them? He does not believe in the one God, who rejects foreign gods. But all the words of Sennacherib were a war of doubt from Satan, before which Hezekiah, who believed in God, was not shaken.
And we notice that the unfaithfulness of the Jews, in their worship of idols on the high places and their setting up of poles, is what made Sennacherib stumble and caused him to blaspheme God.

The strange thing is that Sennacherib casts all these doubts and forgot what had happened to the inhabitants of Samaria, which Assyria took and settled many Gentiles in, and the lions devoured them, and he commanded that a priest of the children of Israel be sent to teach them how to please the god of the land, because he is a mighty god; if he is mighty, why does he cast doubt on him? And why does he not submit to him? But it is the pride of man that leads him to destruction. And this is what actually happened with Sennacherib and all his army, as we shall see in the coming events.

entries.section: (4) Assyria’s threats against Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: And Sennacherib offered a third doubt to Hezekiah about his strength, for he said to him that you have no horsemen to fight, and indeed made an offer to mock him and said to him, I will give you two thousand horses, if you can find two thousand riders to ride upon them, and of course you do not have them, so you are weak and cannot stand before me; surrender and hand over the city.

entries.section: (4) Assyria’s threats against Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: So how can you stand against a single one of the least of the commanders of the king of Assyria, relying on Egypt to supply you with war chariots and horsemen?

entries.section: (4) Assyria’s threats against Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: A fourth doubt is offered by Rabshakeh on behalf of Sennacherib, and he says: And now, do you think that I have come up to destroy this place of my own accord? The Lord is the One who sent me and charged me with laying waste these lands; he lies and claims that God sent him, although Satan is the one who moves him.

Do not believe the doubts of Satan that he sends to you through the mouth of the wicked, or by thoughts within you, for he is a liar and the father of lies. Be sure that all the logical arguments he offers are a false interpretation from himself, as shown by the fact that you are troubled by his words and that his thoughts are all destructive. Drive out his thoughts quickly and seek God and be sure that He is able to protect you from them, however great your weakness.

entries.section: (4) Assyria’s threats against Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: The deputies of Hezekiah feared the effect of the words of the commanders of the king of Assyria on the morale of their soldiers, and so they asked Rabshakeh to speak in Aramaic, which the three deputies of Hezekiah understand, and not to speak in Hebrew, lest the soldiers stationed on the wall and all the people hear and be afraid. Aramaic is the language spoken by the Assyrians and understood by the educated among the Jews, such as the deputies of Hezekiah, while the rest of the Jews know only Hebrew.

entries.section: (4) Assyria’s threats against Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: Their own dung: their waste, that is, their excrement.

Rabshakeh rejected the request of the deputies of Hezekiah and declared the truth of this dialogue, that its aim was not to come to an understanding with Hezekiah but to cast doubt on the soldiers and people of God, so that they would fall into despair and surrender; for the Assyrians would besiege the city until those in it fell into hunger and severe thirst and were compelled to eat their own waste and drink their own urine. And so he began to speak with strong threats and not mere doubts, declaring that if they did not surrender they would certainly die of hunger and thirst.

entries.section: (4) Assyria’s threats against Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: Rabshakeh continued his challenge to the deputies of Hezekiah, and cried with a loud voice in the Hebrew language, directing his words to the soldiers of Judah, calling them to listen to the message of Assyria to them, and he said:

entries.section: (4) Assyria’s threats against Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: Thus says the king: Do not be deceived by what Hezekiah tries to persuade you of, for he is not able to deliver you out of the hand of the king of Assyria.

entries.section: (4) Assyria’s threats against Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: And let not Hezekiah persuade you to trust in the Lord, saying that He will deliver you, so that you do not fall into the hand of the king of Assyria; God is unable to deliver you, and Sennacherib will storm your city.

entries.section: (4) Assyria’s threats against Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: Vine: a grapevine.

Do not listen to him nor believe what he says. Here is the king of Assyria offering you a generous offer, that you declare your surrender to him, and then you will move about freely and live in peace, and every one of you will eat of his own vine and of his fig tree and drink the waters of his own cistern. So after trying to make them doubt, he offers them false happiness and lying promises.

These are the very words of Satan, which he always speaks in the hearts of people, promising them to provide all the means of happiness; woe to the one who listens to him. Is this not what happened with our first parents? And here Sennacherib demands that they come out of Jerusalem, as Satan demands that we come out of the Church and plunge into the lusts of the world to find happiness, though in truth he will enslave us and humble us.

entries.section: (4) Assyria’s threats against Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: Sennacherib continues to deceive the inhabitants of Jerusalem, promising them that he will move them to a fertile land, to enjoy a better life, instead of dying if they obey Hezekiah and do not surrender. The truth is that he will enslave them and move them from their land and scatter them throughout the regions of his kingdom and humble them. Yet whoever examines the words of Sennacherib knows that he is deceitful, for he says that he will move them to a land like their own land, so why should they lose their fertile land? They live in safety under the care of their God. The solution is steadfastness in faith in God, and then the falseness of all the doubts and promises of Sennacherib appears.

entries.section: (4) Assyria’s threats against Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: Was any of the gods of the nations, whose lands the army of the king of Assyria invaded, ever able to repel the king of Assyria? The answer to this is that the gods of the nations are not gods, but God alone is able to protect His people.

entries.section: (4) Assyria’s threats against Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: Hena: the town of Anah on the river Euphrates.
Arpad: a city in Aram whose site today is “Tell Arfad,” at a distance of twenty kilometers north of Hamath.

The Jews who dwelt in the kingdom of Israel, that is, the cities of Samaria, worshiped pagan gods whom Sennacherib mentions here, and Sennacherib thought that these gods had not been able to protect the cities of Samaria because he is stronger than they, and forgot that God, whom the inhabitants of the cities of Samaria had left, was the One who was angry with them for their worship of foreign gods, and so allowed him to attack them and occupy their land. And once more the unfaithfulness of the people of God in the cities of Samaria appears, by their worship of idols, for they caused Sennacherib to blaspheme God and consider Him a weak god, among the gods, unable to resist him.

entries.section: (4) Assyria’s threats against Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: Sennacherib considered God merely one god among the gods, and since all the gods of the nations had been unable to protect their peoples, the God of Israel is therefore unable to protect Jerusalem.

entries.section: (4) Assyria’s threats against Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: None of the soldiers of Judah answered what the commanders of the king of Assyria said; for King Hezekiah had given instructions to everyone to be silent and not to answer the king of Assyria and his commanders anything, lest the effect of doubt on the people increase. And argument with the wicked falls into many sins, for the best thing to do with the thoughts of Satan is to drive them out and not discuss them. This shows the awe in which Hezekiah was held; because he was righteous and feared God, his people respected him and obeyed him and trusted his word.

entries.section: (4) Assyria’s threats against Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: The king’s deputies returned with their clothes rent, in grief at what they had heard, and told King Hezekiah what had been said, for they could not bear the blasphemy of King Sennacherib against God and his casting of doubts on the people.
God triumphs over Sennacherib

entries.section: (1) Hezekiah asks for the prayer of Isaiah, who reassures him

paragraphs.text: When Hezekiah heard Sennacherib's blasphemies against God, he was deeply grieved and tore his clothes, like his three officials, as the last verse of the previous chapter mentions. Hezekiah put on sackcloth, as a sign of his humility, and went to the house of the Lord to cry out to Him, that He might deliver him and defend His holy name. Hezekiah shows how the children of God act in distress before their enemies. When someone threatens the kings of the world with war, they gather their counselors and the commanders of their armies to answer their enemies; Hezekiah, however, took refuge in God before anything else.

entries.section: (1) Hezekiah asks for the prayer of Isaiah, who reassures him

paragraphs.text: Hezekiah sent Eliakim, the master of the palace, and Shebna the scribe, together with the senior priests, clothed in sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah, carrying a message to him from the king. All were grieved at the blasphemy against the name of God. We notice Hezekiah's recourse to Isaiah, the prophet of God: he goes to the house of the Lord and to His prophet, which means that his trust in God is complete, and his reliance upon Him.

We see Hezekiah's concern in sending those who had heard the Assyrian blasphemies, and in sending with them his greatest assistants; he takes refuge in God with all his strength. The king's envoys came to Isaiah and told him Hezekiah's message.

When difficult problems and threats confront you, take refuge in God first, however bewildering the matter may be. Pray, and seek the guidance of your father of confession, and you will hear the voice of God, and He will guide you in everything.

entries.section: (1) Hezekiah asks for the prayer of Isaiah, who reassures him

paragraphs.text: Hezekiah declared through his envoys, who were sent to Isaiah, that the distress they were passing through was very severe, because Sennacherib was stronger than they, and he threatens and blasphemes the name of God, while they are weaker than Sennacherib and cannot answer him; but all their hope is in God, who is able to answer him sharply. He likens the condition of the people to women with child whose time of delivery has come, yet they have no strength for it. They are the people of God, and their God is mighty, able to bring forth the fruit from the womb, that is, to defend His people; and though it has not yet happened, they are waiting for God to intervene.

entries.section: (1) Hezekiah asks for the prayer of Isaiah, who reassures him

paragraphs.text: "It may be that the Lord your God will hear what the Rabshakeh has said, whom his master the king of Assyria sent to reproach the living God, and will rebuke him for the words that he has spoken; so pray for the remnant that survives among us," after the kingdom of Israel was taken captive (ch. 18:10, 11). Nothing was left to Hezekiah but the city of Jerusalem and those in it. So he declares his weakness and his humility before God, that He may have mercy on him and deliver him from the hand of Sennacherib. And certainly God will not forsake the one who takes refuge in Him with faith and humility.

entries.section: (1) Hezekiah asks for the prayer of Isaiah, who reassures him

paragraphs.text: Isaiah reassured Hezekiah's envoys and gave them a message for their king, that he should not be afraid of the servants of the king of Assyria, whom he calls lads, perhaps as a belittling of them and of their power, which is nothing before God. He foretold to them that Sennacherib would hear a rumor that would make him want to return to his own land. This rumor was the advance of Tirhakah king of Ethiopia, his seizing of Egypt, and then his preparing to attack Assyria.

entries.section: (2) The king of Assyria continues his threats

paragraphs.text: Libnah: a city in southern Judah, between Makkedah and Lachish.

The Rabshakeh, the official spokesman for Sennacherib, left the Assyrian army besieging Jerusalem and returned to his king at Lachish, and found that he had left it and gone to fight against Libnah, perhaps hoping that by seizing the city of Libnah, which belonged to Judah, he would weaken Jerusalem and frighten them, so that it would surrender to him.

entries.section: (2) The king of Assyria continues his threats

paragraphs.text: The king of Assyria was told that Tirhakah king of Cush had declared war on him, so he felt the need to seize Jerusalem, in order to strengthen his position against Tirhakah and be free to fight him. He therefore sent to Hezekiah to threaten him and frighten him a second time, since Hezekiah's weakness had appeared before, when he paid silver and gold and declared his submission (ch. 18:14).

entries.section: (2) The king of Assyria continues his threats

paragraphs.text: Although Sennacherib was in extreme fear of Tirhakah, he pretended to be strong and sent to threaten Hezekiah and to make him doubt the power of his God, as though He were unable to protect him from the king of Assyria.

entries.section: (2) The king of Assyria continues his threats

paragraphs.text: Gozan: it lies on the river Habor, north of Babylon, in the Assyrian kingdom.
Haran: it lies near the river Euphrates, on a trade route; caravans came to it from Damascus, Nineveh and Carchemish.
Rezeph: a city located in present-day Iraq, between Hamath and the Euphrates.
The children of Eden: they lived near the river Euphrates, and their capital was Telassar, which means the hill of Assyria.

Arpad, the city of Sepharvaim, Hena and Ivah: see (ch. 17:24, 18:34). The Rabshakeh continued his threats to Hezekiah, reminding him of what the kings of Assyria had done to the peoples who tried to rebel against Assyria, and how they triumphed over them, and the gods of those nations were not able to defend them. Of course, your God will not be able to deliver you, for He is like these gods, powerless before the might of the kings of Assyria.

"Many there be which say of my soul, There is no help for him in God" (Ps 3:2). Beloved, the war is one, though the time differs: it is casting doubt on the power of God and the right hand of His might, so that you lose your faith and your hope... Do not be anxious, but be strengthened; and if the wars weigh heavily upon you, flee to the bosom of your father of confession and the embrace of your Church... there you will find help.

entries.section: (3) The prayer of Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: Hezekiah received the letters of threat from the hands of the messengers of the king of Assyria who had brought them to him, and after he had read their contents he went into the temple and spread them before the Lord.

We notice that the Assyrian threats this time were written, to frighten the children of Israel, but Hezekiah entered the house of the Lord in faith, asking Him to defend His name against the mockery of the nations. He was confident of the power of God, which would work and be glorified.

entries.section: (3) The prayer of Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: Hezekiah prayed before the Lord, saying: O Lord God of Israel, who sit enthroned, borne by the angels, You are the only God of all the peoples of the earth. You made heaven and earth. In this he declared that God alone is God, above the angels and the Creator of the whole world.

entries.section: (3) The prayer of Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: Incline Your ear, O Lord, to the blasphemies of the king of Assyria, and look upon the words of Sennacherib, which he sent to me to reproach You, O God; You alone are the living God.

entries.section: (3) The prayer of Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: It is true, O Lord, what the kings of Assyria have done, laying waste the lands and countries of those peoples and burning their gods, which did not resist, because they are idols and false gods, but the work of men's hands, of wood and stone.

entries.section: (3) The prayer of Hezekiah

paragraphs.text: Hezekiah implored the Lord, saying: Deliver us, O Lord, from the hand of the king of Assyria, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that You alone are the true God. Hezekiah's confidence in God appears in his asking Him to intervene now, that is, quickly, so that His name may be glorified. He is jealous for the name of God and trusts in His power. Out of his love, Hezekiah cannot bear that the name of God be insulted in his presence, and he wants God to show His power, that perhaps the peoples may believe and submit to Him.

Speak with confidence to God in prayer, especially when some mock His power or speak ill of Him, and ask Him to reveal His glory, to support you and to deliver you from all who surround you. For He is above all and able to do all things.

entries.section: (4) The Lord's answer through Isaiah

paragraphs.text: The Lord's answer to the prayer of Hezekiah was swift, for He sent to him through the prophet Isaiah, saying: The Lord has heard what you complained to Him about concerning Sennacherib king of Assyria. This means God's care, and that He will act and protect him and punish those who exalt themselves against him.

entries.section: (4) The Lord's answer through Isaiah

paragraphs.text: Has shaken: shook her head in mockery at the one before her.

God's answer to Hezekiah's prayer was spoken through Isaiah as he addresses Sennacherib. He speaks of the people of God, likening it to a virgin and a maiden: it appears with the weakness of a virgin and a maiden, but its strength is mighty in its God who supports it. This virgin has despised you, Sennacherib, and mocked you. He says this in the past tense because God has decided to take vengeance on Sennacherib and his army, who mocked God; and since God has decided, what He has commanded will surely come to pass, so He spoke in the past tense. For God had used Assyria to discipline His people, that they might repent, but He loves His people very much, so when they cried out to Him with humility, repentance and faith, He hastened to help them and to take vengeance on Assyria, who became proud and thought that its strength was from itself, and did not understand that this was by a temporary permission from God, to discipline the people of God.

entries.section: (4) The Lord's answer through Isaiah

paragraphs.text: God continues His rebuke of Sennacherib, saying to him: How did you dare to mock and blaspheme the Holy One, the God of the children of Israel? Of course these words reached the Assyrian army through some people coming out of Jerusalem, or God declared them through one of the men of Jerusalem from the wall, and the Assyrian army heard them.

entries.section: (4) The Lord's answer through Isaiah

paragraphs.text: Ascent: a road on the top of the heights.
The cedar: a great, hard, tall, evergreen tree, abundant on the mountains of Lebanon.
The cypress: a kind of tall coniferous tree, cone-shaped.
Rugged: a road that is not smoothed, with rocks and stones; but what is meant here is forests that cannot be penetrated because of the density of their trees.
Carmel: a range of mountains covered with dense trees in Lebanon.

God continues and exposes the pride of Sennacherib's arrogant and haughty heart, which exalted itself against the very name of God and against His messengers, that is, Hezekiah's envoys, and boasted that he had invaded all the high countries and the dense forests with their lofty trees, and that no chief or difficult road stood before his chariots, for he cut through and removed every obstacle. Sennacherib wrote these words in his letter to Hezekiah, and God now reveals them to show the extent of his pride.

entries.section: (4) The Lord's answer through Isaiah
